Comparing two groups

Source: vignettes/articles/tutorial-difference.Rmd
tutorial-difference.Rmd
library(MMSpower)

A common question in molecular surveillance is whether the prevalence of a marker differs between two groups: two regions, or the same region before and after an intervention. This article plans such a comparison with design_difference() and then analyses the data with test_difference().

Throughout, the scenario is a drug-resistance marker expected at around 10% in region A (group 1) and 20% in region B (group 2). We want 80% power to detect that difference at the 5% significance level.

How many people, with no clustering?

Start with the simplest case: everyone sampled is independent and the diagnostic test is perfect.

des <- design_difference(prevalence1 = 0.10, prevalence2 = 0.20)
des
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 398
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> NULL
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> NULL
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8000726

The answer is given per group (n_per_group, one value for each group) and as a total (n), with power, the power the rounded design actually achieves. With no clustering this is the same calculation as R’s power.prop.test(), which gives a fractional answer that design_difference() rounds up:

power.prop.test(p1 = 0.10, p2 = 0.20, power = 0.80)$n
#> [1] 198.9634

One-sided or two-sided?

The default, alternative = "two.sided", looks for a difference in either direction. If the only result that would change what you do is region A being lower than region B (or, after an intervention, prevalence going down), a one-sided test is enough, and it needs fewer people:

design_difference(0.10, 0.20, alternative = "less")$n_per_group
#> [1] 157 157

"less" means group 1 lower than group 2; "greater" means group 1 higher. Decide the direction before seeing the data. A one-sided test cannot detect a change in the other direction, however large.

An imperfect test

If the marker assay misses some true positives (sensitivity below 1) or produces some false positives (specificity below 1), the measured prevalences move towards each other. The measured difference is the true difference multiplied by sensitivity + specificity - 1, so a smaller difference has to be detected and more people are needed:

design_difference(0.10, 0.20, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)$n_per_group
#> [1] 317 317

Sensitivity and specificity are assumed to be the same in both groups. That is reasonable when the same laboratory and assay are used for both, and worth checking if they are not.

Clustered sampling

In practice people are sampled at sites (health facilities, villages or schools), and people at the same site tend to be more alike than people at different sites. The intra-cluster correlation (ICC) measures this. The design effect, 1 + (people per site - 1) * ICC, says how many times more people a clustered design needs than an unclustered one.

There are two ways to plan a clustered study. If you know how many people you can sample at each site, fix n_per_site1 (group 2 takes the same value unless you give n_per_site2) and the function solves for the number of sites per group:

d_per <- design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_per_site1 = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_per
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 400 400
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 800
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 20 20
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 20 20
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.95 1.95
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8119198

Each group needs 20 sites of 20 people, 400 people per group and 800 in total.

If the number of sites is fixed instead (for example, the health facilities already in a surveillance network), fix n_sites1 and the function solves for the number of people per site:

d_sites <- design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites1 = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_sites
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 380 380
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 760
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 20 20
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 19 19
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.9 1.9
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 199 199
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.8020484

Each of the 20 sites per group now needs 19 people, 380 people per group and 760 in total.

In both cases n_eff is what each group would need without clustering, and deff is the design effect that turns one into the other.

Groups that differ

The two groups need not share a design. Suppose region B has twice as many sites in the network, and earlier surveys suggest more clustering there. Give each group its own number of sites with n_sites1 and n_sites2, and icc as two values, c(group 1, group 2):

diff_des <- design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites1 = 10, n_sites2 = 20,
                              icc = c(0.02, 0.05))
diff_des
#> $n_per_group
#> [1] 270 540
#> 
#> $n
#> [1] 810
#> 
#> $n_sites
#> [1] 10 20
#> 
#> $n_per_site
#> [1] 27 27
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1.52 2.30
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 155 309
#> 
#> $power
#> [1] 0.800782

Most elements of the result are now pairs of values, one per group; n and power cover the whole study. The people per site is the same in both groups, so region B, with twice the sites, has twice the people. With the same people per site, its larger design effect comes from its higher ICC alone, and its n_eff is about twice region A’s, in the same ratio as the design.

When too few sites cannot reach the target

With the number of sites fixed, adding people to each site helps less and less. Once a site has many people, another person there tells you little that the others have not, because they share the same local conditions. However many are sampled, each site is worth at most 1 / ICC independent people: with an ICC of 0.05, that is 20 people. So 8 sites per group can never give more than 160 independent people per group, which is not enough for 80% power here. The function says so, and reports the highest power that design can reach:

design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites1 = 8, icc = 0.05)
#> Error:
#> ! Target power of 80% cannot be reached with these sites and ICC; the highest power they can give is 70.9%. Increase the number of sites or lower the ICC.

Just above the limit, the answer is possible but not sensible:

design_difference(0.10, 0.20, n_sites1 = 10, icc = 0.05)$n_per_site
#> [1] 3647 3647

Ten sites can give at most 200 independent people per group, barely above the 199 needed, so thousands of people per site are required. If the number of people per site comes out implausibly large, the fix is more sites, not more people.

Analysing the data

Once the data are in, test_difference() tests whether the prevalences differ. It takes the number of positives (x1, x2) and the number tested (n1, n2) at each site in each group.

The data below are simulated, not real: 20 sites per group with 19 people each (the n_sites1 = 20 design above), true prevalences of 10% and 20%, and an ICC of 0.05.

set.seed(2026)
sim_sites <- function(k, size, prev, icc) {
  # site prevalences vary around prev, with the given ICC (beta-binomial)
  a <- prev * (1 / icc - 1)
  b <- (1 - prev) * (1 / icc - 1)
  rbinom(k, size, rbeta(k, a, b))
}
x1 <- sim_sites(20, 19, 0.10, 0.05)
x2 <- sim_sites(20, 19, 0.20, 0.05)
n1 <- n2 <- rep(19, 20)
x1
#>  [1] 2 2 2 1 0 0 2 0 2 0 4 1 4 3 0 7 4 0 3 2
x2
#>  [1] 3 5 2 5 4 9 3 1 3 0 2 3 1 7 3 4 5 3 3 0
res <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2)
res
#> $difference
#> [1] -0.07105263
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] -0.1408457
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] -0.001445529
#> 
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.04579302
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $prevalence1
#> [1] 0.1026316
#> 
#> $prevalence2
#> [1] 0.1736842
#> 
#> $n_eff1
#> [1] 194.5196
#> 
#> $n_eff2
#> [1] 213.5336
#> 
#> $icc1
#> [1] 0.05297391
#> 
#> $icc2
#> [1] 0.04330996
#> 
#> $deff1
#> [1] 1.95353
#> 
#> $deff2
#> [1] 1.779579
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] 36.89077

The estimated difference, group 1 minus group 2, is -7.1 percentage points, with a 95% confidence interval from -14.1 to -0.1. Since no ICC was given, it was estimated from each group’s own sites (icc1, icc2) and used to work out the design effects. An estimated ICC is uncertain, so the test allows for it by using a t distribution in place of the normal, with df degrees of freedom (about 37 here, worked out from the number of sites in each group). With few sites per group this makes the test noticeably more cautious; if a trustworthy value from earlier surveys is available, pass it with icc.

Score or Wald?

The default, method = "score", is the test that design_difference() sizes for. method = "wald" is the simpler textbook test, which works out the standard error from each group’s own prevalence. In large samples the two agree closely:

wald <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2, method = "wald")
rbind(score = unlist(res[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]),
      wald  = unlist(wald[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]))
#>        difference   ci_lower     ci_upper    p_value
#> score -0.07105263 -0.1408457 -0.001445529 0.04579302
#> wald  -0.07105263 -0.1396387 -0.002466565 0.04269457

In small groups, or with prevalences near 0 or 1, the Wald interval can be too narrow, so the score method is the safer default. With either method, the interval leaves out 0 exactly when reject is TRUE.

A one-sided test

If the study was planned as one-sided (region A lower), analyse it that way. The interval is then one-sided too: it runs from -1 up to an upper bound.

one <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2, alternative = "less")
unlist(one[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")])
#>  difference    ci_lower    ci_upper     p_value 
#> -0.07105263 -1.00000000 -0.01338234  0.02289651

An imperfect test

Correcting for sensitivity and specificity changes the estimated prevalences, the difference and its interval, but not the p-value:

imp <- test_difference(x1, n1, x2, n2, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
rbind(perfect   = unlist(res[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]),
      imperfect = unlist(imp[c("difference", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "p_value")]))
#>            difference   ci_lower     ci_upper    p_value
#> perfect   -0.07105263 -0.1408457 -0.001445529 0.04579302
#> imperfect -0.08359133 -0.1657008 -0.001700622 0.04579302

This is expected. With the same test in both groups, the measured prevalences differ exactly when the true ones do, so the evidence for a difference is the same either way. What changes is the size of the true difference that the measured one implies: the measured difference is divided by sensitivity + specificity - 1, which makes the difference larger and its interval wider.
